European Journal of Sustainable Development Research, 10(1), em0363. https://doi.org/10.29333/ejosdr/17557 ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT Received: 13 Aug. 2025 This study aims to examine the role of halal supply chain management (HSCM) in improving sustainability in Accepted: 29 Nov. 2025 micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), by exploring the mediating role of operational efficiency. This study used a quantitative approach with a cross-sectional design. Data were collected from 336 respondents, through a structured questionnaire. Hypothesis testing and mediation models were conducted using structural equation modeling. The research results show that HSCM has a positive impact on sustainability. Furthermore, operational efficiency was shown to significantly mediate the relationship between HSCM and sustainability. These findings indicate that the implementation of halal principles promotes efficiency in business processes, which in turn improves business sustainability. This research provides important insights for culinary businesses to utilize a halal system as a strategy to improve efficiency and sustainability. Practices such as selecting halal- certified suppliers and tracking raw materials can reduce costs and create a sustainable competitive advantage. This study extends existing research by empirically testing the mediating role of operational efficiency in HSCM within MSMEs, a context that has been rarely explored. JSON: Name: hscm_efficiency_sustainability Title: Testing the mediating effect of operational efficiency on the impact of halal supply chain management on sustainability outcomes in culinary MSMEs using structural equation modeling Short Hypothesis: In culinary MSMEs, greater implementation intensity of halal supply chain management practices causes higher operational efficiency, which in turn causes higher sustainability performance. Related Work: Existing research establishes positive associations between halal supply chain management (HSCM), operational efficiency, and firm sustainability using cross-sectional surveys and structural equation models. Prior approaches can be grouped into: (1) survey-based SEM that reports direct HSCM→sustainability links; (2) qualitative/case studies describing best practices for halal traceability and supplier selection; and (3) technological/descriptive studies showing how traceability tools and supplier certification can reduce failure rates. Limitations across prior work include predominant reliance on single-wave self-report data, limited use of objective operational or environmental metrics, convenience sampling of single cities or large firms, weak handling of endogeneity and reverse causality, and under-explored mediation tests with rigorous causal contrasts. As a result, it remains unresolved whether HSCM causally improves sustainability via measured improvements in operational efficiency, how large that mediated effect is, and how robust the pathway is to alternative mediators and identification strategies. Abstract: This research tests whether operational efficiency mediates the causal effect of halal supply chain management (HSCM) implementation on sustainability outcomes in culinary micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). The study combines a multi-site firm-level survey with objective operational and environmental indicators and applies confirmatory structural equation modeling together with causal robustness checks (instrumental variables, propensity-score methods, and difference-in-differences on a panel subset). The primary contribution is a quantified, causal mediation estimate of the HSCM→operational efficiency→sustainability pathway using latent-variable measurement for HSCM and operational efficiency and multiple sustainability outcomes (economic, social, environmental). Expected outcomes include precise path coefficients, mediated effect sizes with bootstrap confidence intervals, and assessment of sensitivity to alternative mediator definitions and identification strategies. Results will provide actionable evidence on whether investments in halal supply chain practices translate into measurable efficiency gains that drive sustainability in culinary MSMEs. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Cross-sectional firm survey of culinary MSMEs across at least four metropolitan regions with target N=1,000; instrument items for HSCM (traceability, halal-certified suppliers, segregation, documentation), operational efficiency (throughput time, waste rate, cost per unit, labor productivity), and sustainability (financial performance, resource use indicators, compliance and community engagement indices). (2) Objective firm-level data subset (N≈400) including monthly sales, energy consumption, raw-material waste, and certification records for two waves 12 months apart (panel N≈400x2). Baselines: (A) SEM direct-effect model (HSCM→sustainability), (B) SEM with operational efficiency mediator, (C) OLS regressions with controls, (D) IV regression using instrument(s) correlated with HSCM but not directly with sustainability (e.g., local halal certification office distance or certification campaign exposure), (E) propensity score matched comparison between high- and low-HSCM adopters, (F) difference-in-differences on panel subset (adopters vs non-adopters over time). Evaluation metrics: standardized path coefficients, mediated effect estimates with bootstrap 5,000 resamples and 95% CIs, R^2 for endogenous constructs, model fit indices (RMSEA, CFI, TLI, χ2/df), AIC/BIC for model selection, average treatment effect (ATE) from PSM, DiD ATT, and predictive RMSE for sustainability outcome models. Experimental setup: latent-variable SEM with multiple indicators per construct, control variables (firm age, size, owner education, region), missing data handled via multiple imputation, bootstrapped mediation significance, robustness checks including (i) replacing operational efficiency with alternative operational metrics (e.g., digitization index), (ii) subgroup analyses by firm size and region, (iii) ablation removing mediator, and (iv) sensitivity to instrument choice and unobserved confounders via Rosenbaum-style bounds. Report effect sizes, p-values, and confidence intervals for all contrasts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: measurement error in self-reported scales and objective metrics; common-method variance when using single-source surveys; weak or invalid instruments causing biased IV estimates; model mis-specification producing misleading SEM path coefficients. Data/evaluation biases: non-random sampling and convenience participation leading to selection bias; social desirability bias in halal and sustainability reporting; survivorship bias if failing firms are excluded. Scalability and compute: limited panel size may reduce power for DiD and IV analyses; complex SEM with many indicators may require large samples to estimate stably. Generalization limits: results from culinary MSMEs in selected regions may not generalize to other sectors, countries, or large firms. Causal limits: residual confounding and reverse causality remain possible when unobserved variables influence both HSCM adoption and sustainability outcomes. Statistical issues: multicollinearity among covariates, sensitivity of fit indices to sample characteristics, and potential overfitting in predictive components.
